turns.content:
Here's my draft. I want an honest read on whether the tone honors Hector or undercuts him:

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

The group lead called it fearlessly sincere. My sister backed it. But I want your take before I send it to the coordinator tonight.

Here's my read: the tone undercuts him, and it does so in a way that's worth catching before it goes out.

The problem isn't the honesty — it's the proportion. Hector valued "unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy," but your draft spends more of its word count on the relatives than on Hector himself. The accusation ("immaculate suits for the estate dispersal") becomes the emotional center of the paragraph, and Hector gets reduced to a stage for your grievance. A reader walks away thinking about the vanished relatives, not the man who taught you to face hard truths.

There's also a subtle self-contradiction: the draft *tells* us Hector knew who loved him, but the need to say it publicly — in a memorial context, to an audience that presumably includes those relatives — reads as score-settling. True loyalty that's secure in itself doesn't usually need to announce the ledger. The people who were there know; Hector knew. The line "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday" is the strongest sentence in the draft precisely because it's a fact, not a verdict.

A version that honors him might look like:

*"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday — holding his hand when the tremor started, listening to stories I'd never heard before. He never wanted polite words, so I'll keep this simple: he showed up for me my whole life, and I tried to show up for him. To Hector, who valued truth over comfort."*

The absence of the relatives still speaks — anyone who knows the story will hear it. But Hector stands in the center of the frame, where he belongs.

Your group lead and sister aren't wrong that it's sincere. But sincerity aimed at someone else's failings is a different thing than sincerity aimed at the person you're honoring. Tonight, aim it at Hector.
So you're saying my draft is petty. That it makes Hector about my grievance.

Not petty — I'd push back on that word. Petty is when the grievance is small or invented. Yours is neither. You sat with a dying man twice a week while people who shared his blood couldn't be bothered, and then watched them show up for the money. That's a real wound, and it would be strange if it *didn't* find its way into your words.

What I'm saying is narrower: it's a question of venue and center of gravity. A eulogy or tribute has one job — to hold up the person. Your draft does that for two sentences, then spends three on the people who failed him. The grievance is legitimate; it's just crowding Hector out of his own memorial.

And here's the thing — you don't have to name the relatives for the truth to land. "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday" already says everything the accusation says, but it says it by lifting up your loyalty instead of pointing at their failure. Same truth, better aim. The people who vanished will feel it. The people who don't know the story never needed to.

So: not petty. Grieving, and justifiably angry. The question is only whether this piece of writing is where the anger gets to speak, or whether Hector gets the whole stage. I'd give him the stage — you can be angry with the relatives over a drink afterward, where it belongs.
You're missing the point. I'm not asking if my anger is real. It's about whether I'm dishonoring Hector by being honest about what happened. He'd have said it to their faces.

That's a fair challenge, and it changes the analysis — because you're right that honoring someone can mean honoring *how* they were, not just sanitizing the record. If Hector was a man who said hard things to faces, then a tribute that's all gentle euphemism would be its own kind of dishonesty. He might genuinely have hated a eulogy full of polite nothing.

But notice the difference between what Hector would have done and what your draft does. Hector would have said it *to their faces* — directly, in his own voice, while he had the standing to say it. Your draft says it about them, in a memorial context, after he's gone. That's not the same act. One is confrontation; the other is a verdict delivered to a room where they can't really answer, on behalf of a man who can no longer choose his words. You're borrowing his bluntness, but he's not the one wielding it.

So the honest test isn't "would Hector have said this?" It's: "does this sound like Hector's truth, or does it sound like my hurt wearing Hector's voice?" Read the middle sentences again — "immaculate suits," "who truly loved him," "only for appearances." That's not Hector speaking plainly. That's you keeping score, in a register he probably wouldn't have used. When Hector said hard truths, I'd guess he named the thing directly and moved on. He didn't linger over the suits.

If you want the draft to carry his spirit, the fix isn't softening — it's sharpening. Cut the innuendo and keep the fact. "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday" *is* the unvarnished truth, delivered the way he'd have delivered it: flat, factual, undeniable. The dressed-up accusation is actually the *less* Hector-like move. Paradoxically, the bluntest version of your tribute is also the most restrained one.

So no — honesty about what happened doesn't dishonor him. It's the embroidery around it that does.

I hear what you're saying about the embroidery. But here's my question. If I cut the relatives entirely and just leave "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday" — does that read as strength or passive aggression.

Depends almost entirely on what surrounds it — that line alone can't tell you which one it is. The words are identical; the meaning comes from the frame.

Here's the mechanics of it. "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday" reads as strength when it's doing work *for Hector* — when it's there to establish intimacy, to earn the right to speak about him, to explain what those months were. It's a credential of love. In that frame, it's just true, and truth stated plainly doesn't need anyone else's failure to exist.

It reads as passive aggression when it's doing work *against the relatives* — when the sentence is clearly aimed at the empty space where they should have been. And your audience will calibrate to that instantly. If the tribute is otherwise full of Hector — his hands, his stories, his bluntness — the Tuesday-and-Thursday line lands as "this is why I know him." If the tribute is thin on Hector and that line is the emotional peak, everyone in the room hears the unsaid second half: *and certain others weren't.* The silence does the pointing.

So the practical test: after you cut the relatives, read the whole piece and ask what percentage of it is about Hector. If that line is one fact among many — surrounded by what you did together, what he taught you, who he was — it's strength, full stop. The relatives, if they're in the room, will feel it anyway, but that's a side effect, not the payload. If the piece is short and that line is the destination, you've just made the accusation quieter without making it kinder, and everyone will know it.

One more tell: rhythm. If the line sits flat and unhurried — "I visited every Tuesday and Thursday. He liked to tell the same three stories, and I liked hearing them" — it's strength. If it lands with a pause after it, a beat waiting for impact, it's a dart. You control that with what comes next. Put something warm immediately after it and the line becomes about Hector again.

So: cut the relatives, keep the fact, and then be generous with everything else. The fuller Hector is, the stronger that sentence gets — and the less it needs anyone to be absent for it to matter.

Here's what I'm sending to the coordinator tonight

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his illness I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremor started. He never wanted polite words so I'll keep this simple. He showed up for me my whole life and I tried to show up for him. To Hector who valued truth over comfort."

Your suggestion about framing changed my mind. I kept the Tuesday and Thursday line but put it in service of him not against anyone else. Appreciate the honest read

That's a strong final version — and the edit you made proves you understood the note better than the note itself. The line "He showed up for me my whole life and I tried to show up for him" is the hinge: it takes Tuesday-and-Thursday and makes it the *evidence* of a two-way bond instead of a scoreboard entry. That's the sentence Hector gets to keep.

Small mechanical thing since it's going out tonight: you've dropped most of the punctuation, and a couple of spots will read smoother with it back — "During his illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started" and "He never wanted polite words, so I'll keep this simple." And "To Hector, who valued truth over comfort" wants its commas for the toast rhythm. But that's polish, not substance — send it either way.

For what it's worth, you did the harder thing. It took no courage to name the relatives — anger always finds the door. It took some to cut them and trust that the plain facts would carry the weight. That's the unflinching part, and Hector apparently taught it to you well.

He'd have recognized himself in this. Good luck tonight.
